120	
121	                                                 During surgery, multiple injured structures are often identified, which may provide insight into the complex
122	                                                 pathophysiology of sports hernias. These injured structures can include the ones listed below [9].
123	
124	
125	                                                 Distal rectus abdominis: The distal portion of the rectus abdominis muscle, which is part of the abdominal
126	                                                 musculature, may be subject to injury due to the aforementioned imbalances.
127	
128	
129	                                                 Conjoint tendon: This structure, which connects the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles to
130	                                                 the pubic bone, can also be affected in sports hernia cases.
131	
132	
133	                                                 External oblique aponeurosis: The external oblique aponeurosis, a broad, flat tendon that connects the
134	                                                 external oblique muscle to the pubic bone, can become damaged due to repetitive stresses from athletic
135	                                                 activities. The ilioinguinal nerve runs adjacent to the external oblique aponeurosis before entering the
136	                                                 external inguinal ring and has been similarly implicated in the symptomatology of sports hernias [10].
137	
138	
139	                                                 Inguinal ligament: The inguinal ligament, which forms the base of the inguinal canal, may also be
140	                                                 compromised in cases of sports hernias. This ligament plays a crucial role in supporting the inguinal region
141	                                                 and can be subject to injury when subjected to excessive stress.
142	
143	
144	                                                 Adductor longus muscle/tendon: The adductor longus, a hip adductor muscle that is often stronger in
145	                                                 individuals with sports hernias, may also be injured due to the excessive forces placed on it during sports
146	                                                 activities. This muscle injury could exacerbate the imbalance between the abdominal and hip adductor
147	                                                 muscles, thereby increasing the risk of a sports hernia.
148	
149	
150	                                                 Matrix Metalloproteinases and Genetic Underpinnings
151	
152	
153	                                                 Although athletic pubalgia is a separate entity from classic inguinal hernias, the two might not be
154	                                                 completely disparate in their underlying mechanisms. Recent studies are casting light on the shared
155	                                                 foundations they might have, particularly concerning the structural soundness of the extracellular matrix
156	                                                 and the possible role of genetics in predisposition. The structural integrity of the extracellular matrix is
157	                                                 paramount for maintaining tissue resilience, especially in areas subjected to repetitive stresses, such as the
158	                                                 inguinal region. A study spearheaded by the University of Naples Federico II has turned the spotlight on the
159	                                                 role of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in these vulnerabilities [11]. Elevated levels of MMPs in hernia-
160	                                                 affected tissues hint at a potential weakening or compromise of the matrix, which might be instrumental in
161	                                                 hernia onset. The interplay between these MMPs and their natural inhibitors, tissue inhibitors of
162	                                                 metalloproteinases (TIMPs), is equally significant. An imbalance between MMPs and TIMPs could pave the
163	                                                 way for structural vulnerabilities, making this axis a potential target of interest in understanding the
164	                                                 pathophysiology of both inguinal hernias and athletic pubalgia.
165	
166	
167	
168	
169	2023 Kopscik et al. Cureus 15(8): e43283. DOI 10.7759/cureus.43283                                                                                                2 of 9
170	                                                  Genetics seems to be playing its part in the broader conversation as well. A pioneering publication in Nature
171	                                                 Communications unveiled specific genetic regions associated with hernia susceptibilities, emphasizing their
172	                                                 quintessential roles in preserving the structural fidelity of connective tissues [12]. Notably, Genome-Wide
173	                                                 Association Studies (GWAS) have been pivotal in deciphering these genetic markers, painting a clearer
174	                                                 picture of how genetics might interplay with tissue vulnerabilities [13]. This begs an intriguing question: Are
175	                                                 there unique genetic footprints that make certain individuals more susceptible to athletic pubalgia? The
176	                                                 tapestry of research around inguinal hernias offers a repository of insights, many of which can be transposed
177	                                                 to understand athletic pubalgia better. The dynamic between MMPs and TIMPs, coupled with the emerging
178	                                                 genetic insights, might just be the tip of the iceberg. As research forges ahead, we can anticipate a future
179	                                                 where our grasp of athletic pubalgia deepens, potentially leading to precise diagnostic tools, tailored
180	                                                 therapeutic interventions, and preemptive measures for those in the crosshairs of sports hernias.
181	
182	
183	                                                 Risk factors and prevention
184	                                                 Understanding the risk factors and potential preventative measures for sports hernias is essential for
185	                                                 clinicians to effectively manage and treat this condition. Athletic pubalgia occurs predominantly in sports
186	                                                 that require sudden and forceful movements. Sports hernias have been observed to be particularly common
187	                                                 in those involved in activities that demand sudden acceleration, deceleration, kicking, cutting, twisting, and
188	                                                 turning. These activities place significant stress on the muscles, tendons, and ligaments in the groin and
189	                                                 lower abdomen, increasing the likelihood of injury [14]. Sports with the highest risk of sports hernias include
190	                                                 soccer, hockey, football, rugby, and track and field events such as sprinting and hurdling [15]. Athletes in
191	                                                 these sports are particularly susceptible to sports hernias due to the frequent and intense demands on their
192	                                                 lower abdominal and groin regions.
193	
194	
195	                                                 To minimize the risk of sports hernias, it is crucial to address the underlying factors that contribute to their
196	                                                 development. Strength and conditioning programs that emphasize flexibility, core strength, and sport-
197	                                                 specific movements have been suggested as possible preventative measures [16]. These programs should be
198	                                                 tailored to the individual athlete, taking into account their specific sport, skill level, and physical condition.
199	                                                 One potential contributing factor to sports hernias is a strength imbalance between the musculature below
200	                                                 the pubic symphysis and the muscles above it. Strengthening the abdominal oblique and rectus muscles may
201	                                                 help to correct this imbalance and, in turn, reduce the risk of injury [17]. However, it is important to note
202	                                                 that research in this area is currently lacking, and more studies are needed to confirm the effectiveness of
203	                                                 these targeted strengthening exercises in preventing sports hernias. In addition to targeted strength and
204	                                                 conditioning programs, athletes should also focus on proper warm-up and cool-down routines, as well as
205	                                                 sport-specific drills to improve their technique and movement efficiency [17]. Properly fitted and supportive
206	                                                 footwear may also play a role in reducing the risk of injury by providing adequate stability and cushioning
207	                                                 during high-impact activities.
208	
209	
210	                                                 History and presenting symptoms
211	                                                 The common history of present illness features in sports hernias or athletic pubalgia involves activity-
212	                                                 related pain that is relieved with rest but returns upon resumption of sports. The pain typically has a gradual
213	                                                 onset, worsens over time, and may affect daily activities. It is crucial for clinicians to consider these features
214	                                                 when evaluating patients presenting with groin pain and to explore potential coexisting conditions to
215	                                                 ensure a comprehensive assessment and appropriate treatment plan. Sports hernias typically present with a
216	                                                 distinct set of symptoms related to the history of the patient’s illness, and the most common features
217	                                                 include those listed below [7,10].
218	
219	
220	                                                 Activity-related pain: Affected individuals usually experience lower abdominal and proximal adductor-
221	                                                 related pain during activities that involve quick acceleration, deceleration, kicking, twisting, or lateral
222	                                                 movement. Soccer players, in particular, may develop sports hernias as a result of hard or long kicks.
223	
224	
225	                                                 Relief with rest: The pain associated with sports hernias tends to be relieved with rest but often returns once
226	                                                 individuals resume their sport.
227	
228	
229	                                                 Gradual onset: Sports hernias can develop gradually over time, but they may also occur suddenly after a
230	                                                 tearing sensation is felt during physical activity.
231	
232	
233	                                                 Pain progression: In the early stages of a sports hernia, pain is typically felt after the activity or toward the
234	                                                 end of the activity. As the condition worsens, the pain becomes more severe and starts to occur earlier in the
235	                                                 activity, leading to a decreased ability to twist, turn, or stride out. Eventually, the pain may be present during
236	                                                 running and can progress to affect daily activities.
237	
238	
239	                                                 Pain distribution: Sports hernias are usually unilateral, but the pain may radiate to the uninvolved side or the
240	                                                 scrotum.
241	
242	
243	                                                 Exacerbating factors: The pain associated with sports hernias can be reproduced by sudden movements, sit-
244	                                                 ups, coughing, sneezing, and the Valsalva maneuver.
245	
246	
247	
248	
249	2023 Kopscik et al. Cureus 15(8): e43283. DOI 10.7759/cureus.43283                                                                                                    3 of 9
250	                                                  Hip joint-related mechanical symptoms: It is important for clinicians to inquire about any hip joint-related
251	                                                 mechanical symptoms, such as catching, locking, and giving way, which may be indicative of underlying
252	                                                 issues.
253	
254	
255	                                                 Physical examination features
256	                                                 The physical examination is a crucial component in the evaluation of sports hernias, also known as athletic
257	                                                 pubalgia. A thorough examination helps in differentiating sports hernias from other causes of groin pain.
258	                                                 The essential physical examination technique involves the inversion of the scrotal skin and palpation along
259	                                                 the inguinal canal. A diagnosis of sports hernia may be made if at least three of the following five signs are
260	                                                 present [9]: (1) Pinpoint tenderness to the pubic tubercle at the conjoint tendon insertion. (2) Tenderness
261	                                                 over the deep inguinal ring. (3) Pain and/or dilation of the external ring without a palpable hernia. (4) Pain at
262	                                                 the origin of the adductor longus tendon. (5) Dull, diffuse groin pain that often radiates to the perineum and
263	                                                 inner thigh or across the midline.
264	
265	
266	                                                 In addition to these signs, a complete examination for other causes of groin pain should be performed: (1)
267	                                                 Hip adductor origin tenderness and pain with resisted adduction suggest adductor-related groin pain. (2)
268	                                                 Tenderness at the pubic symphysis indicates pubic-related groin pain. (3) Pain with resisted hip flexion
269	                                                 and/or stretching of hip flexors suggests iliopsoas-related groin pain. (4) Hip joint-related groin pain may be
270	                                                 identified by eliciting pain during passive range of motion (ROM) tests, such as flexion, adduction, and
271	                                                 internal rotation (FADIR), as well as flexion, abduction, and external rotation (FABER) tests. (5) A
272	                                                 genitourinary examination should be performed to rule out other potential causes of groin pain.
273	
274	
275	                                                 Differential diagnosis
276	                                                 When diagnosing sports hernias or athletic pubalgia, it is crucial for clinicians to consider a range of possible
277	                                                 differential diagnoses. These conditions may present with similar symptoms, such as groin pain or
278	                                                 discomfort, but require different management and treatment approaches. Some of the key differential
279	                                                 diagnoses to consider include the ones listed below.
280	
281	
282	                                                 Inguinal or femoral hernia: Characterized by a palpable mass with appropriate maneuver, these hernias can
283	                                                 cause groin pain similar to sports hernias. Physical examination techniques, such as the Valsalva maneuver,
284	                                                 may help to identify these hernias.
285	
286	
287	                                                 Hip adductor strain [18]: Pain with resisted action of the adductor muscles may indicate a hip adductor
288	                                                 strain, which can mimic sports hernia symptoms. Clinical assessment and imaging, such as ultrasound or
289	                                                 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), can help differentiate this condition from athletic pubalgia.
290	
291	
292	                                                 Rectus abdominis strain: This muscle strain in the abdomen can cause pain similar to sports hernias and
293	                                                 may be confused with athletic pubalgia. A thorough clinical examination and imaging studies can help
294	                                                 distinguish between the two conditions.
295	
296

During surgery, multiple injured structures are often identified, which may provide insight into the complex
                                                 pathophysiology of sports hernias. These injured structures can include the ones listed below [9].


                                                 Distal rectus abdominis: The distal portion of the rectus abdominis muscle, which is part of the abdominal
                                                 musculature, may be subject to injury due to the aforementioned imbalances.


                                                 Conjoint tendon: This structure, which connects the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles to
                                                 the pubic bone, can also be affected in sports hernia cases.


                                                 External oblique aponeurosis: The external oblique aponeurosis, a broad, flat tendon that connects the
                                                 external oblique muscle to the pubic bone, can become damaged due to repetitive stresses from athletic
                                                 activities. The ilioinguinal nerve runs adjacent to the external oblique aponeurosis before entering the
                                                 external inguinal ring and has been similarly implicated in the symptomatology of sports hernias [10].


                                                 Inguinal ligament: The inguinal ligament, which forms the base of the inguinal canal, may also be
                                                 compromised in cases of sports hernias. This ligament plays a crucial role in supporting the inguinal region
                                                 and can be subject to injury when subjected to excessive stress.


                                                 Adductor longus muscle/tendon: The adductor longus, a hip adductor muscle that is often stronger in
                                                 individuals with sports hernias, may also be injured due to the excessive forces placed on it during sports
                                                 activities. This muscle injury could exacerbate the imbalance between the abdominal and hip adductor
                                                 muscles, thereby increasing the risk of a sports hernia.


                                                 Matrix Metalloproteinases and Genetic Underpinnings


                                                 Although athletic pubalgia is a separate entity from classic inguinal hernias, the two might not be
                                                 completely disparate in their underlying mechanisms. Recent studies are casting light on the shared
                                                 foundations they might have, particularly concerning the structural soundness of the extracellular matrix
                                                 and the possible role of genetics in predisposition. The structural integrity of the extracellular matrix is
                                                 paramount for maintaining tissue resilience, especially in areas subjected to repetitive stresses, such as the
                                                 inguinal region. A study spearheaded by the University of Naples Federico II has turned the spotlight on the
                                                 role of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in these vulnerabilities [11]. Elevated levels of MMPs in hernia-
                                                 affected tissues hint at a potential weakening or compromise of the matrix, which might be instrumental in
                                                 hernia onset. The interplay between these MMPs and their natural inhibitors, tissue inhibitors of
                                                 metalloproteinases (TIMPs), is equally significant. An imbalance between MMPs and TIMPs could pave the
                                                 way for structural vulnerabilities, making this axis a potential target of interest in understanding the
                                                 pathophysiology of both inguinal hernias and athletic pubalgia.




2023 Kopscik et al. Cureus 15(8): e43283. DOI 10.7759/cureus.43283                                                                                                2 of 9
                                                  Genetics seems to be playing its part in the broader conversation as well. A pioneering publication in Nature
                                                 Communications unveiled specific genetic regions associated with hernia susceptibilities, emphasizing their
                                                 quintessential roles in preserving the structural fidelity of connective tissues [12]. Notably, Genome-Wide
                                                 Association Studies (GWAS) have been pivotal in deciphering these genetic markers, painting a clearer
                                                 picture of how genetics might interplay with tissue vulnerabilities [13]. This begs an intriguing question: Are
                                                 there unique genetic footprints that make certain individuals more susceptible to athletic pubalgia? The
                                                 tapestry of research around inguinal hernias offers a repository of insights, many of which can be transposed
                                                 to understand athletic pubalgia better. The dynamic between MMPs and TIMPs, coupled with the emerging
                                                 genetic insights, might just be the tip of the iceberg. As research forges ahead, we can anticipate a future
                                                 where our grasp of athletic pubalgia deepens, potentially leading to precise diagnostic tools, tailored
                                                 therapeutic interventions, and preemptive measures for those in the crosshairs of sports hernias.


                                                 Risk factors and prevention
                                                 Understanding the risk factors and potential preventative measures for sports hernias is essential for
                                                 clinicians to effectively manage and treat this condition. Athletic pubalgia occurs predominantly in sports
                                                 that require sudden and forceful movements. Sports hernias have been observed to be particularly common
                                                 in those involved in activities that demand sudden acceleration, deceleration, kicking, cutting, twisting, and
                                                 turning. These activities place significant stress on the muscles, tendons, and ligaments in the groin and
                                                 lower abdomen, increasing the likelihood of injury [14]. Sports with the highest risk of sports hernias include
                                                 soccer, hockey, football, rugby, and track and field events such as sprinting and hurdling [15]. Athletes in
                                                 these sports are particularly susceptible to sports hernias due to the frequent and intense demands on their
                                                 lower abdominal and groin regions.


                                                 To minimize the risk of sports hernias, it is crucial to address the underlying factors that contribute to their
                                                 development. Strength and conditioning programs that emphasize flexibility, core strength, and sport-
                                                 specific movements have been suggested as possible preventative measures [16]. These programs should be
                                                 tailored to the individual athlete, taking into account their specific sport, skill level, and physical condition.
                                                 One potential contributing factor to sports hernias is a strength imbalance between the musculature below
                                                 the pubic symphysis and the muscles above it. Strengthening the abdominal oblique and rectus muscles may
                                                 help to correct this imbalance and, in turn, reduce the risk of injury [17]. However, it is important to note
                                                 that research in this area is currently lacking, and more studies are needed to confirm the effectiveness of
                                                 these targeted strengthening exercises in preventing sports hernias. In addition to targeted strength and
                                                 conditioning programs, athletes should also focus on proper warm-up and cool-down routines, as well as
                                                 sport-specific drills to improve their technique and movement efficiency [17]. Properly fitted and supportive
                                                 footwear may also play a role in reducing the risk of injury by providing adequate stability and cushioning
                                                 during high-impact activities.


                                                 History and presenting symptoms
                                                 The common history of present illness features in sports hernias or athletic pubalgia involves activity-
                                                 related pain that is relieved with rest but returns upon resumption of sports. The pain typically has a gradual
                                                 onset, worsens over time, and may affect daily activities. It is crucial for clinicians to consider these features
                                                 when evaluating patients presenting with groin pain and to explore potential coexisting conditions to
                                                 ensure a comprehensive assessment and appropriate treatment plan. Sports hernias typically present with a
                                                 distinct set of symptoms related to the history of the patient’s illness, and the most common features
                                                 include those listed below [7,10].


                                                 Activity-related pain: Affected individuals usually experience lower abdominal and proximal adductor-
                                                 related pain during activities that involve quick acceleration, deceleration, kicking, twisting, or lateral
                                                 movement. Soccer players, in particular, may develop sports hernias as a result of hard or long kicks.


                                                 Relief with rest: The pain associated with sports hernias tends to be relieved with rest but often returns once
                                                 individuals resume their sport.


                                                 Gradual onset: Sports hernias can develop gradually over time, but they may also occur suddenly after a
                                                 tearing sensation is felt during physical activity.


                                                 Pain progression: In the early stages of a sports hernia, pain is typically felt after the activity or toward the
                                                 end of the activity. As the condition worsens, the pain becomes more severe and starts to occur earlier in the
                                                 activity, leading to a decreased ability to twist, turn, or stride out. Eventually, the pain may be present during
                                                 running and can progress to affect daily activities.


                                                 Pain distribution: Sports hernias are usually unilateral, but the pain may radiate to the uninvolved side or the
                                                 scrotum.


                                                 Exacerbating factors: The pain associated with sports hernias can be reproduced by sudden movements, sit-
                                                 ups, coughing, sneezing, and the Valsalva maneuver.




2023 Kopscik et al. Cureus 15(8): e43283. DOI 10.7759/cureus.43283                                                                                                    3 of 9
                                                  Hip joint-related mechanical symptoms: It is important for clinicians to inquire about any hip joint-related
                                                 mechanical symptoms, such as catching, locking, and giving way, which may be indicative of underlying
                                                 issues.


                                                 Physical examination features
                                                 The physical examination is a crucial component in the evaluation of sports hernias, also known as athletic
                                                 pubalgia. A thorough examination helps in differentiating sports hernias from other causes of groin pain.
                                                 The essential physical examination technique involves the inversion of the scrotal skin and palpation along
                                                 the inguinal canal. A diagnosis of sports hernia may be made if at least three of the following five signs are
                                                 present [9]: (1) Pinpoint tenderness to the pubic tubercle at the conjoint tendon insertion. (2) Tenderness
                                                 over the deep inguinal ring. (3) Pain and/or dilation of the external ring without a palpable hernia. (4) Pain at
                                                 the origin of the adductor longus tendon. (5) Dull, diffuse groin pain that often radiates to the perineum and
                                                 inner thigh or across the midline.


                                                 In addition to these signs, a complete examination for other causes of groin pain should be performed: (1)
                                                 Hip adductor origin tenderness and pain with resisted adduction suggest adductor-related groin pain. (2)
                                                 Tenderness at the pubic symphysis indicates pubic-related groin pain. (3) Pain with resisted hip flexion
                                                 and/or stretching of hip flexors suggests iliopsoas-related groin pain. (4) Hip joint-related groin pain may be
                                                 identified by eliciting pain during passive range of motion (ROM) tests, such as flexion, adduction, and
                                                 internal rotation (FADIR), as well as flexion, abduction, and external rotation (FABER) tests. (5) A
                                                 genitourinary examination should be performed to rule out other potential causes of groin pain.


                                                 Differential diagnosis
                                                 When diagnosing sports hernias or athletic pubalgia, it is crucial for clinicians to consider a range of possible
                                                 differential diagnoses. These conditions may present with similar symptoms, such as groin pain or
                                                 discomfort, but require different management and treatment approaches. Some of the key differential
                                                 diagnoses to consider include the ones listed below.


                                                 Inguinal or femoral hernia: Characterized by a palpable mass with appropriate maneuver, these hernias can
                                                 cause groin pain similar to sports hernias. Physical examination techniques, such as the Valsalva maneuver,
                                                 may help to identify these hernias.


                                                 Hip adductor strain [18]: Pain with resisted action of the adductor muscles may indicate a hip adductor
                                                 strain, which can mimic sports hernia symptoms. Clinical assessment and imaging, such as ultrasound or
                                                 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), can help differentiate this condition from athletic pubalgia.


                                                 Rectus abdominis strain: This muscle strain in the abdomen can cause pain similar to sports hernias and
                                                 may be confused with athletic pubalgia. A thorough clinical examination and imaging studies can help
                                                 distinguish between the two conditions.


                                                 Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) [19]: This condition, caused by abnormal contact between the femoral
                                                 head and acetabulum, can lead to groin pain and may be mistaken for a sports hernia. Physical examination,
                                                 including provocative tests, and imaging studies such as X-ray or MRI, can help identify FAI.


                                                 Osteitis pubis [20]: Inflammation of the pubic symphysis can cause chronic groin pain, which may be
                                                 confused with athletic pubalgia. Diagnostic imaging, such as X-ray, MRI, or bone scintigraphy, can help
                                                 differentiate osteitis pubis from sports hernias.


                                                 Bursitis: Inflammation of a bursa near the hip joint can cause pain that may mimic sports hernia symptoms.
                                                 A thorough clinical examination and imaging studies can help identify bursitis and distinguish it from
                                                 athletic pubalgia.

312	                                                 Snapping hip syndrome: This condition, characterized by a snapping or clicking sensation in the hip during
313	                                                 movement, can cause groin pain and can be mistaken for a sports hernia. Physical examination, including
314	                                                 assessment of the hip ROM and palpation of the hip joint, can help identify snapping hip syndrome.
315	
316	
317	                                                 Diagnostic workup and testing
318	                                                 Sports hernias can be challenging to diagnose due to the variety of potential causes and the often
319	                                                 nonspecific nature of symptoms. In addition, athletic pubalgia often coexists with other causes of chronic
320	                                                 groin pain [16]. While a thorough physical examination remains crucial for the diagnosis of sports hernias
321	                                                 and should always be performed, the role of additional diagnostic tests will be discussed in this section. It is
322	                                                 important to note that athletic pubalgia is a clinical diagnosis, and cannot be ruled out by any single
323	                                                 imaging study [21]. This section will provide a comprehensive overview of the diagnostic tests and
324	                                                 interpretations used to identify sports hernias and related conditions. Most patients with this condition will
325	                                                 have no pathologic imaging findings. However, these tests can still be helpful in ruling out other potential
326	                                                 causes of groin pain.
327	
328	
329	2023 Kopscik et al. Cureus 15(8): e43283. DOI 10.7759/cureus.43283                                                                                                   4 of 9
330	                                                  Magnetic Resonance Imaging
331	
332	
333	                                                 MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality to evaluate for sports hernias. Specific patterns of injury have
334	                                                 been identified, including tears of the rectus abdominis and adductor aponeurosis [7] as well as erosion
335	                                                 and/or osteitis of the pubic bodies (Figure 1). However, these findings are not specific to athletic pubalgia.
336	                                                 Similar to radiographs, MRI is often used to exclude alternative causes of chronic groin pain due to its high
337	                                                 sensitivity in identifying injury to adjacent structures [9].
338	
339	
340	
341	
342	                                                    FIGURE 1: Axial (A) and coronal (B) T2 fat saturation MRI images
343	                                                    through the symphysis pubis.
344	                                                    A: T2 axial imaging displays an amplified signal within and around the anterosuperior segment of the pubic body
345	                                                    (red arrow). This signal is discernible directly under the insertion point of the common adductor-rectus abdominis
346	                                                    aponeurosis, indicating long-term tendon and bone interface disruption. B: Tear of the adductor longus muscle
347	                                                    tendon (white arrow) from the symphysis with slight retraction and fluid (white signal) between the tendon and
348	                                                    bone.
349	
350	
351	
352	
353	                                                 When ordering an MRI for a suspected sports hernia, clinicians should request a dedicated pelvis MRI with
354	                                                 attention to the pubic symphysis and surrounding soft tissue structures. This imaging protocol should
355	                                                 include T1-weighted and T2-weighted (including fat saturation) sequences in multiple planes. Axial and
356	                                                 oblique axial as well as coronal planes are most contributory. The use of intravenous contrast may be
357	                                                 beneficial in cases with subtle imaging findings to better visualize any inflammation or injury to the
358	                                                 involved structures [22]. To assure focused imaging, clinicians must communicate their specific clinical
359	                                                 suspicion for a sports hernia to the radiologist, as this will likely influence protocol selection as well as the
360	                                                 radiologist’s interpretation of the images.
361	
362	
363	                                                 Dynamic Ultrasound
364	
365	
366	                                                 Dynamic ultrasound is increasingly utilized in the evaluation of posterior inguinal wall insufficiency, which
367	                                                 is commonly seen in sports hernias. This noninvasive imaging modality offers several advantages, such as
368	                                                 real-time assessment, minimal discomfort, and the ability to evaluate structures during different phases of
369	                                                 movement. However, the presence of posterior inguinal wall insufficiency has low sensitivity and specificity
370	                                                 for diagnosing sports hernias, as it may also be observed in asymptomatic athletes [23]. Furthermore,
371	                                                 ultrasound is highly operator dependent and has limited availability. During an ultrasound examination, a
372	                                                 skilled sonographer can identify various features associated with sports hernias. These features include soft
373	                                                 tissue abnormalities such as anechoic defects and/or partial or full-thickness discontinuities of the tendon
374	                                                 insertions, indicative of tears; loss of normal fibrillary architecture, thickening, and hypoechogenicity of
375	                                                 tendon insertions, suggestive of tendinopathy. Bone changes may include spurring and irregularities of the
376	                                                 pubic bone, indicative of chronic stress or injury; symphyseal effusion, representing joint inflammation or
377	                                                 injury; and periarticular hyperemia on color Doppler, revealing increased blood flow around the affected
378	                                                 area. Reproduction of symptoms on the pressure with the ultrasound transducer is especially valuable to
379	                                                 confirm the location of pain or discomfort [24]. However, there are potential pitfalls in the ultrasound
380	                                                 assessment for sports hernias. Anisotropy, an artifact that occurs when the angle of the ultrasound beam
381	                                                 relative to the tendon fibers changes, can result in the false appearance of tendinosis. Correct positioning of
382	                                                 the transducer and using appropriate settings can help minimize this artifact. Additionally, protrusion of
383	
384	
385	2023 Kopscik et al. Cureus 15(8): e43283. DOI 10.7759/cureus.43283                                                                                                       5 of 9
386	                                                  pre-peritoneal fat through the Hesselbach triangle during abdominal strain can mimic the appearance of a
387	                                                 hernia. Recognizing this finding and differentiating it from a true sports hernia is crucial for accurate
388	                                                 diagnosis.
389	
390	
391	                                                 Radiographs
392	
393	
394	                                                 Diagnostic workup for sports hernias often involves the use of radiographs as a first-line imaging modality in
395	                                                 the sports medicine clinic. These imaging techniques can provide valuable insights into the underlying
396	                                                 causes of groin pain, helping physicians to diagnose or exclude sports hernias and other conditions that
397	                                                 might contribute to discomfort in the region [25]. For example, radiographs may reveal alternative diagnoses
398	                                                 including fractures, degenerative disease, FAI, dysplasia, and pubic symphysis asymmetry [26]. Additionally,
399	                                                 alignment abnormalities, such as pelvic tilt or leg length discrepancies that can contribute to groin pain and
400	                                                 muscular imbalances, may be identified on standing radiographs.
401	
402	
403	                                                 Computed Tomography Scan
404	
405	
406	                                                 Computed tomography (CT) scans can provide more detailed information on bony structures and soft tissues
407	                                                 surrounding the groin area. These scans can help identify the widening of the symphysis pubis, a potential
408	                                                 indicator of pubic instability or stress injuries, which may contribute to the development of sports hernias or
409	                                                 cause similar symptoms to a sports hernia. Additional findings of reactive sclerosis, marginal erosion,
410	                                                 and/or capsular thickening are supportive findings. CT scans can also assist in excluding other causes of
411	                                                 groin pain, such as osteoarthritis or FAI, by providing a more precise analysis of joint spaces, cartilage, and
412	                                                 bony morphology [27,28]. Identifying these conditions may help guide appropriate treatment and prevent
413	                                                 unnecessary interventions for a sports hernia.
414	
415	
416	                                                 Herniography
417	
418	
419	                                                 Herniography is an invasive diagnostic test that involves the injection of contrast material into the
420	                                                 peritoneal cavity to visualize the inguinal region. Although highly sensitive and specific at diagnosing “true”
421	                                                 hernias, herniography is generally not recommended as a first-line diagnostic tool for sports hernias due to
422	                                                 its invasive nature [29].
423	
424	
425	                                                 Nuclear Medicine Bone Scintigraphy
426	
427	
428	                                                 Nuclear medicine bone scan is not typically indicated for the diagnosis of athletic pubalgia. Although this
429	                                                 modality is exquisitely sensitive to the pathology of the bony skeleton and readily detects fractures,
430	                                                 osteoarthritis, and osteomyelitis, the resolution is insufficient to differentiate reactive osteitis and fracture,
431	                                                 for example. Further, the lack of soft tissue analysis precludes the evaluation of marginal tendons and the
432	                                                 aponeurotic condensation, anatomic structures that must be evaluated in this clinical setting [30].
433	
434	
435	                                                 Treatment
436	                                                 General Measures
437	
438	
439	                                                 Nonoperative treatment should be attempted before surgical consideration, as conservative management is
440	                                                 often successful in managing sports hernias. This typically includes a nonsurgical rehabilitation treatment
441	                                                 plan consisting of an initial six- to eight-week period of rest with supportive care, such as nonsteroidal anti-
442	                                                 inflammatory drugs, ice, and heat [7,31]. After this period, a six-week rehabilitation program with a gradual
443	                                                 return to sports activity is recommended [31].
444	
445	
446	                                                 The rehabilitation program should initially focus on hip adductor stretching and core stabilization exercises,
447	                                                 before advancing to eccentric strengthening of abdominal oblique, rectus abdominis, and adductors [16,17].
448	                                                 Finally, the program should progress to sports-specific functional exercises. The entire process may take as
449	                                                 long as two to three months. Ultrasound-guided injection to rectus abdominis insertion, conjoint tendon, or
450	                                                 adductor tendon may be considered, but there is limited evidence for its efficacy [17].
451	
452	
453	                                                 Surgery/Other Procedures
454	
455	
456	                                                 Surgery should be considered if nonoperative treatment fails after three or more months [17]. Herniorrhaphy
457	                                                 is the definitive treatment for sports hernias. Although surgical techniques vary, the general principles are
458	                                                 to release abnormal tension on the inguinal canal and reinforce the posterior wall of the inguinal canal [32].
459	                                                 There are two main types of surgery for sports hernias, namely, open and laparoscopic techniques.
460	
461	
462	                                                 Open surgery involves a larger incision, and while it has been reported to be effective, it may be associated
463	                                                 with a longer recovery time compared to laparoscopic surgery [33]. Laparoscopic surgery, on the other hand,
464	                                                 involves smaller incisions and allows for a quicker return to sport [34]. Both open and laparoscopic surgical
465	                                                 techniques have been reported to be effective at similar rates [17].
466	
467	
468	
469	2023 Kopscik et al. Cureus 15(8): e43283. DOI 10.7759/cureus.43283                                                                                                    6 of 9
470	                                                  Return to Sport
471	
472	
473	                                                 Returning to sport following treatment for athletic pubalgia, whether pursued through conservative or
474	                                                 surgical avenues, is shaped by the treatment’s modality, individualized factors, and injury severity. The time
475	                                                 to fully return to sports ranges from four to 12 weeks depending on the type of surgery and individual
476	                                                 recovery factors [32]. Post-surgery, the rate of return to the prior level of activity is reported to be between
477	                                                 80% and 95% [35,36]. To optimize surgical outcomes, it is essential that clinicians and patients carefully
478	                                                 consider the most appropriate surgical approach based on the patient’s specific condition, preferences, and
479	                                                 goals.
480	
481	
482	                                                 Trends drawn from recent literature suggest that return-to-play (RTP) timelines, while variable, lean toward
483	                                                 promising outcomes. For instance, in a surgical approach tailored for athletic pubalgia by Kajetanek and
484	                                                 colleagues, an impressive 92.6% of subjects made a successful RTP to their pre-injury sport levels within an
485	                                                 average span of 112 ± 38 days. It is noteworthy that athletes with sole lower abdominal wall injuries reported
486	                                                 a swifter recovery, clocking in at about 91.1 ± 21.0 days, particularly when contrasted with their counterparts
487	                                                 who sustained only adductor tendon injuries or a combination of injuries [37]. Diving deeper into the realm
488	                                                 of professional sports, Castle et al. identified that a substantial 90.91% of NBA players resume play after
489	                                                 their surgical intervention for athletic pubalgia, albeit within a slightly protracted average timeline of 4.73 ±
490	                                                 2.62 months. However, a caveat looms over this statistic; these athletes have been observed to experience a
491	                                                 contraction in their career longevity subsequent to the surgery [38]. Expanding the scope, Serafim et al.,
492	                                                 through a comprehensive review, inferred that athletes opting for surgery often rejoin their sport sooner
493	                                                 than those adopting conservative treatments. Yet, they underscore the primacy of weighing conservative
494	                                                 strategies before leaping to surgical decisions [39].
495	
496	
497	                                                 Mirroring investigations and discourses from other athletic milieus, the overarching narrative points toward
498	                                                 commendable RTP rates, often transcending the 90% mark, post-treatment for athletic pubalgia. It is
499	                                                 imperative, however, to not merely assess RTP in isolation but to juxtapose it with athletes’ capacities to
500	                                                 revert to their pre-injury prowess and gauge it against their contemporaries. Despite occasional
501	                                                 discrepancies in the data regarding post-surgical game involvement and proficiency in professional sports
502	                                                 spheres, a consensus is building around the optimistic potential for athletes to retrace their path back to
503	                                                 full-fledged gameplay and performance, especially in the aftermath of surgical intervention for athletic
504	                                                 pubalgia.
505	
506	
507	                                                 Conclusions
508	                                                 Sports hernias continue to present a significant challenge for clinicians due to their complex and
509	                                                 multifaceted nature. Accurate diagnosis and effective treatment of sportsman’s hernia necessitate a careful

{
 "id": "Q89",
 "sourceFile": "Specificity and Areas of Usage of Cardiovascular Prediction Models Among Athletes—State-of-the-art Review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title Specificity and Areas of Usage of Cardiovascular Prediction Models Among Athletes matches the filename, and the article's own DOI 10.31083/RCM37493 is printed on page 1.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Endurance Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative state-of-the-art review of cardiovascular prediction models for atrial fibrillation, hypertension, coronary artery disease, cardiomyopathies and VO2max as they apply to athletes, mainly endurance athletes. No sample is analysed and no search method is described; the authors propose a four-phase protocol that uses risk scores to decide when a fuller medical evaluation is needed.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No systematic search, inclusion rule or quality appraisal is described, so the choice of models cannot be reproduced. The authors state that most models were derived in general populations, many have not been externally validated in athletes, and the conclusions are often preliminary and based on small observational studies.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the proposed screening protocol as a validated clinical pathway for athletes, when the authors present it as an untested proposal and state that prediction models cannot make a final diagnosis.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Chomiuk T, Kasiak P, Mamcarz A, Śliż D. Specificity and Areas of Usage of Cardiovascular Prediction Models Among Athletes—State-of-the-art Review. Rev Cardiovasc Med. 2025;26(5):37493.",
  "doi": "10.31083/RCM37493",
  "abstract": "Summarizes the practical use of common prediction models for maximal oxygen uptake, cardiac arrhythmias, hypertension, atherosclerosis and cardiomyopathies in athletes, with a focus on endurance disciplines. The authors also propose a pre-participation protocol for applying these models.",
  "tldr": "Cardiovascular risk models can help decide which athletes need a fuller medical check before progressive training. The authors present them as a screening aid rather than a diagnosis, and most have not been validated in athletes.",
  "methods": "Narrative state-of-the-art review. No systematic search, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal are described.",
  "findings": "The authors summarize atrial fibrillation scores (CHARGE-AF was judged most suitable for preliminary screening in European populations), Framingham-based hypertension scores and exercise blood pressure regression equations, and coronary artery disease models. They note that hypertension is more common in strength than endurance disciplines and that AF prevalence in middle-aged and master athletes has been reported at 12% to 29%. They recommend adding VO2max and other fitness indicators to future models.",
  "limitations": "Narrative design with no described search method. Most models come from general populations, many lack external validation in athletes, and the authors identify gaps in ethnic and non-European representation. Several recommendations are described as preliminary.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use a validated risk score as a first-pass screen to flag athletes who need a full clinical evaluation before intense or progressive training, and record the flag. Do not treat a score as a diagnosis, and recognize that most scores have not been validated in athletes.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Risk and exercise-capacity screening can help set safe training intensity zones for amateur, master and professional endurance athletes, with a medical referral when risk is flagged.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review touches on return-to-play guidance for athletes with confirmed or suspected cardiovascular disease, but it gives no outcome data on return timelines. It cannot set a return-to-play decision alone and depends on the treating physician's assessment."
 }
}

 "sourceFile": "Spikes in acute-chronic workload ration associated with a 5-7 times greater injury rate in English Premier League football players - A comprehensive 3-year study.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title in the text, Spikes in acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) associated with a 5-7 times greater injury rate in English Premier League football players, matches the filename (which misspells ratio as ration), and the article's own DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2018-099422 is printed in the running header.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Training & Performance", "Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Observational analysis of GPS workload and time-loss injury records for 33 outfield players at one English Premier League club across three seasons (2014/15 to 2016/17), with 132 injuries and 61 player-seasons analysed. A very high acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR above 2.0) combined with low chronic load gave non-contact injury relative risks of about 4.5 to 6.6 depending on the metric, while contact injuries were linked to moderate to high ratios (RR 2.0 to 2.6).",
 "screeningLimitations": "One club, 33 players, and 61 player-seasons treated as independent observations limit generalization. Match data for 2014/15 were estimated, about 11% of sessions lacked data and were imputed, goalkeepers were excluded, and the authors did not calculate power prospectively.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 5 to 7 times figure as the injury risk of any workload spike, when it applies to non-contact injuries within specific low-chronic-load subgroups, and the study shows association rather than proof that spikes cause injury.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "Bowen L, Gross AS, Gimpel M, Bruce-Low S, Li FX. Spikes in acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) associated with a 5–7 times greater injury rate in English Premier League football players: a comprehensive 3-year study. Br J Sports Med. 2020;54:731-738.",
  "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2018-099422",
  "abstract": "Examined the relation between GPS-derived workloads and injury in 33 English Premier League players over three seasons. Cumulative loads and acute:chronic workload ratios were classified by z-scores and relative risk was calculated for injured versus non-injured players. Non-contact injury risk was highest when chronic exposure was low and the ACWR exceeded 2.0. The authors recommend monitoring the ACWR and avoiding spikes that approach or exceed 2.0.",
  "tldr": "In this one-club study, sudden jumps in training load (ACWR above 2.0) on top of low chronic load were linked to the highest non-contact injury risk. The authors recommend building chronic load gradually and avoiding spikes near 2.0.",
  "methods": "Analysis of GPS workload (StatSports Viper units, video-based match data from 2015/16) and club-recorded injury data over three seasons. Cumulative 1- to 4-week loads and ACWR were classified by z-scores, relative risks were estimated with binary logistic regression, and only conditions with 20 or more injuries were analysed.",
  "findings": "For all injuries, a low chronic load of accelerations, decelerations or low-intensity distance combined with a very high ACWR gave RR 2.8 to 3.5. For non-contact injuries, a very high ACWR with low chronic load gave RR 4.5 (total distance) to 6.6 (decelerations), and with all chronic loads the very high ACWR gave RR 3.7 to 3.9. Overall injury risk with a very high ACWR across all chronic loads was RR 2.4 to 2.6. Contact injuries were linked to moderate to high ACWR (RR 2.0 to 2.6), and 80% of contact injuries occurred in matches.",
  "limitations": "The abstract gives RR 6.7 for ACWR above 2.0 with low decelerations, while the results text and Table 5 give RR 6.6 at ACWR above 2.3; the abstract and text should be read together. The title range of 5 to 7 times rests on subgroup results, and the lowest value for total distance is 4.5. Other limits: 2014/15 match data were estimated, 11% of sessions were imputed, 61 player-seasons were treated as independent, sub-threshold injury cells were dropped, and only external load was measured.",
  "practicalImplications": "Track the ACWR alongside cumulative load and avoid week-to-week spikes that approach or exceed 2.0, especially when chronic load is low. Build chronic load progressively, because the authors note that reducing load to lower risk can also cost fitness.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Use weekly GPS load and ACWR to plan progressions for squad members, avoiding spikes near 2.0 and building chronic load gradually before match-level demands.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study does not address return to play. Its ACWR thresholds describe in-season injury risk in healthy squad players and cannot set loading after an injury."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q91",
 "sourceFile": "Sport Hernias - A comprehensive review for clinicians.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title Sport Hernias: A Comprehensive Review for Clinicians matches the filename, and the article's own DOI 10.7759/cureus.43283 is printed on page 1.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative clinical review of sports hernias (athletic pubalgia) covering epidemiology, proposed pathogenesis, history and examination, imaging, nonoperative and surgical treatment, and return to sport. No sample is analysed and no search method is described; the return-to-sport figures are quoted from individual studies, with reported return to prior activity of 80% to 95% after surgery.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No search strategy, sources or inclusion rules are described, so the evidence base cannot be reproduced. The authors acknowledge that the pathophysiology is unclear, and the return-to-play figures they quote come from selected surgical and professional groups.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 80% to 95% return-to-prior-activity figure as an expected outcome for any athlete, when it comes from selected surgical series, and the review gives both a claim that conservative care is often successful and a conclusion that response to conservative treatment is disappointingly low.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Kopscik M, Crisman JL, Lomasney L, Smith S, Jadidi S. Sports Hernias: A Comprehensive Review for Clinicians. Cureus. 2023;15(8):e43283.",
  "doi": "10.7759/cureus.43283",
  "abstract": "Reviews current knowledge on sports hernias, a cause of chronic groin pain in athletes, covering pathogenesis, diagnostic approaches and management. The authors argue that the condition needs a multidisciplinary approach and further research.",
  "tldr": "Sports hernia is a clinical diagnosis of chronic groin pain in athletes, and no single imaging study rules it out. Nonoperative rehabilitation is tried first, and surgery is considered when it fails after about three months.",
  "methods": "Narrative clinical review. No search strategy, databases or inclusion criteria are described.",
  "findings": "The authors describe men as more than 90% of cases, with soccer the most common sport. They report that a diagnosis is made when at least three of five examination signs are present, that MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality, and that the posterior inguinal wall was deficient in 85% of surgical cases in one cited study. Nonoperative care is a rest period of six to eight weeks followed by about six weeks of graded rehabilitation. Return to full sport is given as four to 12 weeks depending on treatment type.",
  "limitations": "Narrative design with no described search, so the evidence base is not transparent. The authors state that dynamic ultrasound has low sensitivity and specificity, that the benefit of targeted strengthening for prevention is not established, and that prospective randomized surgical studies are needed. Return-to-play figures come from selected case series.",
  "practicalImplications": "Make the diagnosis clinically, examining for the adductor, pubic and inguinal signs and ruling out hip, pubic and hernia causes before ordering imaging. Start with rest and graded rehabilitation, and consider a surgical opinion if symptoms persist beyond about three months.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Athletes with groin pain need early assessment for a sports hernia so that core and hip adductor work can be planned; the review says the evidence that targeted strengthening prevents sports hernias is lacking.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The 4- to 12-week return range and the staged rehabilitation sequence can frame expectations after nonoperative or surgical care. The reported return rates come from selected groups, and the review gives no criteria for individual clearance."
 }
}

 "sourceFile": "Sport and exercise genomics - The FIMS 2019 consensus statement update.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title Sport and exercise genomics: the FIMS 2019 consensus statement update matches the filename, and the article's own DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2019-101532 is printed in the header.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Consensus / Position Statement",
 "primaryDomain": "Athlete Wellbeing",
 "domains": ["Athlete Wellbeing", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Research & Analytics", "Sports Medicine", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "International consensus update of a guiding reference for sport and exercise genomics, built from a SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats) analysis by 20 authors. It reports no athlete sample and no empirical data; it sets out recommendations on ethics, data protection, genetic counselling, replication and the use of athletes' genomic information.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The document is a SWOT-based guidance text with no described consensus method, such as a Delphi process or voting, so its recommendations reflect expert judgement. The authors note that most sport and exercise genetic associations lack replication in independent populations.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the document as evidence that genetic tests can predict injury or performance, when it states that most sport genetic variants have not been replicated and have no current clinical utility.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "Tanisawa K, Wang G, Seto J, Verdouka I, Twycross-Lewis R, Karanikolou A, et al. Sport and exercise genomics: the FIMS 2019 consensus statement update. Br J Sports Med. 2020 (epub ahead of print).",
  "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2019-101532",
  "abstract": "Updates a previous consensus on sport and exercise genomics using a SWOT analysis and develops a guiding reference covering the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats of the field, with emphasis on ethics, data protection and athlete privacy.",
  "tldr": "Genetic information from athletes has real potential, but most sport genetic findings are unreplicated. The guidance calls for replication studies, privacy safeguards and genetic counselling before genetic information is used for athletes.",
  "methods": "Consensus update built on a SWOT analysis. No sample, search protocol or formal voting method is reported.",
  "findings": "The authors state that most sport and exercise gene associations have not been replicated, that polygenic traits need very large samples (about 5,500 cases and as many controls to detect an odds ratio of 1.2 in a case-control GWAS), and that genetic testing may help evaluate athletes with abnormal cardiac screening or a family history of inherited cardiac disease. They list threats including re-identification of anonymised genotype data, inaccurate testing based on thin evidence, discrimination and gene doping.",
  "limitations": "The statement is an expert guidance document rather than an evidence synthesis, and the consensus process is not described. The authors acknowledge small samples and limited replication in the field, and say the guidance will be updated as evidence emerges.",
  "practicalImplications": "Before collecting athlete genetic data, plan consent, data protection and genetic counselling for results that could be misread. Treat sport genetic findings as research hypotheses until they are replicated.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: The guidance does not support using genetic markers to select sports or set training. It says that selecting sports from a few variants is unlikely to be possible because athletic performance is polygenic.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The statement does not address return to play. Its genetic-testing remarks concern evaluating athletes with abnormal cardiac screening or a family history of inherited cardiac disease."
 }
}
