{
 "id": "Q94",
 "sourceFile": "Sport-related structural brain injury and return to play - Systematic review and expert insight.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title Sport-Related Structural Brain Injury and Return to Play: Systematic Review and Expert Insight matches the filename, and the article's own DOI 10.1093/neuros/nyab041 is printed in the header.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury", "Brain Health & Psychology"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Youth / Adolescent", "Collegiate", "Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary": "PRISMA-based systematic review of PubMed records on sport-related structural brain injury from 2012 onward: 241 records screened and 27 studies included, almost all case reports or series, of which only 12 athletes from 9 articles had return-to-play information. A survey of 31 of 32 invited sports neurosurgeons (96.9%) found that 12 (38.7%) would not operate on an acute, asymptomatic structural injury, and most allowed return to high-contact sport at 6 to 12 months after resolved hemorrhage.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The systematic review yields 27 studies, almost all of them case reports with level 4 evidence, and the survey reflects opinion from one specialist group, 71% of whom were US-based. A single reviewer screened records with senior verification, and the protocol was not registered.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the expert survey percentages, such as 6 to 12 months before return to high-contact sport, as an evidence-based return timeline, when they rest on 12 athletes' case reports and surgeon opinion, and the authors describe the responses as heterogeneous.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2021,
  "citation": "Zuckerman SL, Yengo-Kahn AM, Tang AR, Bailes JE, Beauchamp K, Berger MS, et al. Sport-Related Structural Brain Injury and Return to Play: Systematic Review and Expert Insight. Neurosurgery. 2021.",
  "doi": "10.1093/neuros/nyab041",
  "abstract": "Combines a focused PRISMA systematic review of sport-related structural brain injury from 2012 onward with a cross-sectional survey of 31 international sports neurosurgeons on operative management and return to play. The authors conclude that return-to-play decisions are heterogeneous and that level of play matters.",
  "tldr": "Return to play after sport-related structural brain injury has no evidence-based guidance, and expert opinion varies widely. Experts allowed earlier return at higher levels of play, and most allowed high-contact sport at 6 to 12 months after resolved hemorrhage.",
  "methods": "Focused systematic review following PRISMA, using PubMed MeSH terms and keywords; titles and abstracts from 2012 onward were screened, full texts reviewed by one author and verified by a senior author, and the protocol was not registered. A cross-sectional online survey covered 3 experience questions and 13 multiple-choice questions on operative indications and return timing in four scenarios at high school, collegiate and professional levels.",
  "findings": "Of 241 records, 27 studies were included. Nine articles (12 athletes) reported return-to-play information, and 10 of those 12 cases were high school athletes or younger. Among 31 responding neurosurgeons, 12 (38.7%) would not operate on an acute, asymptomatic structural injury; midline shift over 10 mm (63.2%) and hemorrhage over 10 mm (52.6%) were the most common operative indications among those who would. For resolved hemorrhage, most experts allowed return to high-contact sport at 6 to 12 months, and about 80% did not endorse return to high-contact sport with persistent hemorrhage. After craniotomy, 40% to 50% considered return at 6 to 12 months. Linear regression found that experts allowed earlier return at higher levels of play (beta -0.58, P = .033).",
  "limitations": "The systematic review yields little (27 studies, 12 athletes with return data), and the survey reflects opinion rather than outcomes. The regression is printed as beta -0.58 with 95% CI -0.111 to -0.005, which places the point estimate outside its own interval; this inconsistency appears in both the abstract and the results and should be checked against the source. The authors also note heterogeneity in both the literature and the survey responses.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use the paper as a structured aid for individualized decisions rather than a return-to-play protocol. Note the authors' finding that experts were more lenient at higher competition levels, and that they were more conservative after craniotomy or with persistent hemorrhage.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: The review does not inform training load. Its only performance-relevant point is that expert views on return timing varied with level of play, so athletes at higher competition levels need individual planning with the treating neurosurgeon.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Use it to frame the range of expert opinion on operative indications and return timing, such as 6 to 12 months for high-contact sport after resolved hemorrhage and no return for persistent hemorrhage in about 80% of experts. It cannot replace individual neurological and imaging assessment, and the evidence base is 12 athletes plus opinion."
 }
}

 "primaryDomain": "Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains": ["Nutrition & Hydration", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Nutrition", "Athletic Training", "Coaching", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Endurance Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified", "Youth / Adolescent"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Sports Dietitians Australia position statement on nutrition and hydration for exercise in hot and humid environments, written by sports nutrition and sports science researchers and practitioners. It reviews heat stress physiology, gastrointestinal function, fluid and sodium losses and heat acclimation, then gives practical strategies and sport-specific recommendations for team, endurance, junior, travelling and para-sport athletes. It reports no new data.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a consensus document. It does not describe a systematic search or grade the evidence behind each recommendation, so the strength of support for each strategy cannot be read from the text.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the sodium loading, hyperhydration and cold-beverage strategies as proven performance tools for every athlete, when the statement presents them as options to tailor to individual sweat losses, gut tolerance and event rules.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "McCubbin AJ, Allanson BA, Caldwell Odgers JN, Cort MM, Costa RJS, Cox GR, et al. Sports Dietitians Australia Position Statement: Nutrition for Exercise in Hot Environments. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2020 (ahead of print).",
  "doi": "10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0300",
  "abstract": "Position of Sports Dietitians Australia that exertional heat stress challenges athletes' nutritional status, health and performance.  "evidenceSummary": "Perspective piece tracing historical and current research on fluid and carbohydrate intake during endurance exercise, plus a pilot study of 16 well-trained Kenyan runners on a 25.1 km run (about 95 minutes at roughly 2,000 m altitude) who drank ad libitum. Runners lost a mean of 4.2 ± 1.0% of body mass (range 2.2% to 5.9%), and no gastrointestinal distress was reported with any drink, including an alginate hydrogel carbohydrate drink.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The piece is a perspective with no described literature search.  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the alginate hydrogel drink as an established performance product, when the authors state that its effect on carbohydrate oxidation and gastric emptying still needs confirmation and that the marathon winners' use is only indirect evidence.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Sutehall S, Muniz-Pardos B, Bosch AN, Di Gianfrancesco A, Pitsiladis YP. Sports Drinks on the Edge of a New Era. Curr Sports Med Rep. 2018;17(4):112-116.",
  "doi": "",
  "abstract": "No abstract is printed. The perspective traces how fluid and carbohydrate recommendations for exercise have changed, outlines current research on carbohydrate mixes, and describes a pilot study of an alginate hydrogel delivery system in Kenyan runners.",
  "tldr": "Fluid and carbohydrate advice has moved from replacing all sweat loss toward tolerating some dehydration and optimizing carbohydrate mixes. The alginate hydrogel system is promising but unproven, so the usual 30 to 60 g per hour carbohydrate guidance still applies until it is tested.",
  "methods": "Perspective article combining a historical review of the literature with a short pilot field study (16 runners, 25.1 km run) that measured body mass change and fluid intake.",
  "findings": "The perspective describes the 1996 advice to match fluid loss, the 2007 ACSM statement allowing a level of tolerable dehydration, and the evidence that carbohydrate intake of 30 to 60 g per hour improves prolonged endurance exercise (up to 90 g per hour for ultra-endurance events). It cites a review proposing carbohydrate beverages of 5.0% to 6.9% for running performance. In the pilot, runners lost 4.2 ± 1.0% of body mass and reported no gastrointestinal distress; the three athletes using the alginate drink consumed 291.3 ± 26.4 mL over 95 minutes.",
  "limitations": "This is a perspective rather than a structured review, with no search method. The pilot is small and partly inconsistent (four athletes described as receiving the alginate drink, three analysed, one dataset omitted). The authors state that the alginate system's efficacy is not yet confirmed, and their evidence that elite marathon winners used the drink comes from a press report.",
  "practicalImplications": "Keep carbohydrate intake within 30 to 60 g per hour for endurance events unless the athlete has tolerated more, and plan fluid intake around tolerated losses rather than a fixed 2% body mass limit. Treat alginate hydrogel drinks as a promising option to trial with monitoring, not an established one.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Use the carbohydrate range and individualized fluid plans. Trial new high-carbohydrate delivery systems only in training, monitoring gut comfort and body mass.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Not addressed. The piece concerns fluid and carbohydrate intake during endurance exercise and does not address return after injury or illness."
 }
}
